title: van Emde Boas Trees

sections.heading: The Predecessor Problem Over a Bounded Universe
sections.body:
The van Emde Boas (vEB) structure solves the *dynamic predecessor problem*: maintain a subset $S$ of the universe $U=\{0,1,\dots,u-1\}$ under Insert, Delete and Member, while also answering Minimum, Maximum, Successor and Predecessor — "what is the next element of $S$ above (or below) a query key $x$" — all in $O(\lg\lg u)$ time. This is strictly more than a hash table gives: hashing answers Member in expected $O(1)$ but cannot answer Successor at all, since it destroys order.

The starting point is the direct-access table idea from the symbol-table lecture: if keys are drawn from $U$ and you allocate an array $T[0..u-1]$ with $T[k]=x$ when $x\in S$ and $key(x)=k$, every operation is $\Theta(1)$ — including Successor, by scanning forward. The catch, spelled out in the same lecture, is that $U$ is usually far too big to allocate: 64-bit keys alone already give $u=2^{64}=18{,}446{,}744{,}073{,}709{,}551{,}616$ possible values. A vEB tree keeps the direct-access table's $O(1)$-ish flavour while cutting the *time* to $O(\lg\lg u)$ — small enough that a 64-bit universe needs only $\lg\lg u=6$ — by never materializing the full array, and building it instead as a recursive tree of size-$\sqrt u$ direct-access tables.

sections.heading: Representation: a Recursive √u Split
sections.body:
Assume, as CLRS does, that $u=2^{2^k}$ for some $k$, so $\sqrt u$ is again a universe size of the same form; this keeps the split's arithmetic exact across levels. A vEB structure $V$ of universe size $u$ stores $V.min$ and $V.max$ — the current extremes of $S\cap[0,u)$, or NIL if empty — and, when $u>2$, an array $V.cluster[0..\sqrt u-1]$ of $\sqrt u$ recursive vEB structures of size $\sqrt u$, plus one more size-$\sqrt u$ vEB structure $V.summary$.

Split $x\in[0,u)$ into $high(x)=\lfloor x/\sqrt u\rfloor$ (which cluster) and $low(x)=x\bmod\sqrt u$ (position inside it), with $index(i,j)=i\sqrt u+j$ as the inverse. $x\in S$ iff $low(x)\in V.cluster[high(x)]$ — with one exception, which is the representation invariant: **$V.min$ and $V.max$ are never themselves stored inside a cluster.** Cluster $i$ is non-empty iff $i\in V.summary$, so "is there a non-empty cluster to the right of $i$" is itself a predecessor query — on a universe of size $\sqrt u$, exactly the same problem one level smaller. The base case is $u=2$: a single bit, held by min/max alone, with no cluster or summary.

The min/max invariant is the detail every first implementation gets wrong: because the minimum is cached rather than recursed into, the very first element inserted into an empty structure costs $O(1)$ at every level it would otherwise have touched — there is nothing beneath it yet to update.

sections.heading: Operations, and How They Restore the Invariant
sections.body:
**Member($x$)**: true if $x\in\{V.min,V.max\}$; otherwise, for $u>2$, recurse into $V.cluster[high(x)]$ with key $low(x)$.

**Insert($x$)**: (1) if $V.min=$ NIL the structure was empty — set $V.min=V.max=x$ and stop, no recursion. (2) Otherwise, if $x<V.min$, swap $x$ and $V.min$: the new value becomes the cached minimum, and the *old* minimum — which until now existed only in the cache, never in a cluster — is the value that actually gets inserted recursively. (3) For $u>2$, let $i=high(x)$, $j=low(x)$: if $V.cluster[i]$ is empty, insert $i$ into $V.summary$ (a real recursive call) and set $V.cluster[i].min=V.cluster[i].max=j$ directly, with no recursive call into the cluster, since that is exactly the state a fresh one-element cluster should have; if $V.cluster[i]$ is already non-empty, recurse Insert into it with $j$ and leave the summary untouched, since $i$ is already marked there. (4) If $x>V.max$, set $V.max=x$.

The branch in step 3 is load-bearing: the summary insert and the cluster insert are never both "real" size-$\sqrt u$ recursive calls in the same invocation. Delete is the mirror image — removing $x$ may empty $V.cluster[i]$, which then has to be deleted from $V.summary$ too, and if $x$ was $V.min$ or $V.max$, the new extreme has to be pulled back up out of the cluster/summary structure.

**Successor($x$)** either answers from the current cluster or jumps clusters via the summary: if $low(x)$ is below the maximum of cluster $high(x)$, the answer lies inside that same cluster (one recursive call); otherwise the next non-empty cluster is $Successor(V.summary,high(x))$ (also one recursive call), and the answer is that cluster's Minimum. Predecessor is symmetric, with one extra fallback: if no earlier cluster holds anything smaller, the answer is $V.min$ itself — again, because the minimum is invisible inside every cluster.

sections.heading: Why O(lg lg u): the Recurrence
sections.body:
Every operation above does $O(1)$ work at the current level plus **at most one** recursive call into a structure of universe size $\sqrt u$: Insert never makes two "real" recursive calls, and Successor/Predecessor never look into more than one cluster before falling back to the summary. That gives the recurrence
$$T(u) = T(\sqrt u) + O(1)$$
Writing $m=\lg u$ turns the repeated square-rooting of $u$ into repeated halving of $m$, an ordinary $T(m)=T(m/2)+O(1)$ recurrence, so $T(u)=O(\lg m)=O(\lg\lg u)$.

The mutual exclusion in Insert's step 3 is exactly what keeps this a single-recursion recurrence. Drop it — call Insert on both $V.summary$ and $V.cluster[high(x)]$ unconditionally, which might look like the "obvious" way to write it — and inserting into an already-populated cluster re-inserts an already-marked index into the summary, which now recurses further down instead of hitting the $O(1)$ empty-structure base case: $T(u)=2T(\sqrt u)+O(1)=\Theta(\lg u)$, correct but no faster than a balanced tree.

$O(\lg\lg u)$ is genuinely small: for $u=2^{64}$, $\lg\lg u=\lg 64=6$ — six levels of recursion, against 64 comparisons for a balanced BST over the same universe.

sections.heading: The Space Problem, and the Fix: x-fast and y-fast Tries
sections.body:
Every level allocates a cluster array and a summary sized by $\sqrt u$ whether or not anything is stored there, so a vEB tree's space is $\Theta(u)$ regardless of how many elements $n$ it actually holds — for a 32-bit universe that is already on the order of $2^{32}$ words to store even a handful of keys, and a 64-bit universe is simply not buildable.

Willard's **x-fast trie** attacks a related bound from a different angle: store the $n$ keys as leaves of a conceptual binary trie of depth $\lg u$, and at each of the $\lg u$ levels keep a hash table mapping present prefixes to nodes, each caching the nearest descendant leaf below it. A query binary-searches the $\lg u$ levels for the lowest one at which the query's prefix is present, using $O(\lg\lg u)$ hash lookups; space is $O(n\lg u)$, and because it is hash-based, $O(\lg\lg u)$ is expected rather than worst-case.

The **y-fast trie** removes the remaining $\lg u$ factor in space: partition the sorted keys into $\Theta(n/\lg u)$ groups of $\Theta(\lg u)$ consecutive keys, keep each group in its own balanced BST — search inside a group is $O(\lg\lg u)$ because a group has only $\Theta(\lg u)$ elements — and run an x-fast trie over just one representative per group. That trie now has $O(n/\lg u)$ leaves, so total space is $O(n)$; rebalancing group boundaries after an insert or delete costs $O(\lg u)$ but only once every $\Theta(\lg u)$ updates, so it is $O(\lg\lg u)$ amortized. Net result: $O(\lg\lg u)$ expected/amortized time in $O(n)$ space — the vEB tree's time bound without its space bill.

sections.heading: Engineering Notes
sections.body: Straight vEB trees see essentially no production use: $\Theta(u)$ space and a chain of pointer-chasing recursive calls (roughly one cache miss per level) make a B-tree or a hash table faster in practice despite the worse asymptotics, and $u$ has to be known in advance and of the right power-of-two-of-a-power-of-two form. What does survive into real systems is the recursive $\sqrt n$-way split itself, reused as a *static memory layout* rather than a dynamic ADT: the van Emde Boas layout for a balanced binary search tree stores the top $\sqrt n$ levels of the tree contiguously, then recursively lays out each of the $\sqrt n$ subtrees the same way. That layout is the standard technique behind cache-oblivious search trees, giving good cache behaviour at every block size $B$ simultaneously without the tree ever being told what $B$ is.

code.caption: A vEB tree over universe size u = 2^(2^k): Member, Insert and Successor, verified against the u=16 worked example.

worked_example.problem: Build a vEB tree over universe size $u=16$ ($\sqrt u=4$) by inserting $2,3,5,7,14,15$ in that order, then trace $\text{Successor}(7)$.
worked_example.solution:
With $u=16$: $high(x)=\lfloor x/4\rfloor$, $low(x)=x\bmod4$.

**Insert 2** into an empty structure hits the $V.min=$ NIL case directly: $V.min=V.max=2$, nothing else touched.

**Insert 3**: $3\ge V.min(2)$, no swap. $high(3)=0$, $low(3)=3$; cluster 0 is empty, so insert $0$ into the summary (its first element too — another direct hit) and set $cluster[0].min=cluster[0].max=3$ directly. $3>V.max(2)$, so $V.max=3$.

**Insert 5**: $high(5)=1$, $low(5)=1$; cluster 1 is empty $\Rightarrow$ insert $1$ into the summary (which recurses one level inside the summary itself) and set $cluster[1].min=cluster[1].max=1$. $V.max=5$.

**Insert 7**: $high(7)=1$, $low(7)=3$; cluster 1 is now *non-empty* ($min=1$) $\Rightarrow$ recurse Insert(cluster 1, 3) instead of touching the summary; inside cluster 1, $3\ge1$ and its own sub-cluster is empty, so $cluster[1].max$ becomes $3$. $V.max=7$.

**Insert 14, 15** land in cluster 3 the same way: 14 finds cluster 3 empty ($low(14)=2$, direct hit, summary gains index 3), 15 finds cluster 3 non-empty and recurses ($low(15)=3$). $V.max=15$.

Final state: $V.min=2$ (cached, never in a cluster), $V.max=15$; cluster 0 holds low-value $\{3\}$ (element 3), cluster 1 holds low-values $\{1,3\}$ (elements 5, 7), cluster 2 is empty, cluster 3 holds low-values $\{2,3\}$ (elements 14, 15); summary $=\{0,1,3\}$.

**Successor(7)**: $7\ge V.min$, so check cluster $high(7)=1$: its max is $3$, and $low(7)=3$ is *not* less than $3$, so the answer is not inside cluster 1. Jump via the summary: $Successor(summary,1)=3$, the next marked index after 1. The answer is $index(3,\ Minimum(cluster[3]))=index(3,2)=3\cdot4+2=14$ — matching the sorted set $\{2,3,5,7,14,15\}$, where 14 is the element right after 7.

pitfalls: Assuming Insert is $O(\lg u)$ because it 'looks like' it touches both the summary and a cluster at every level — the $O(\lg\lg u)$ bound only holds because the cluster-empty case is short-circuited into a direct min/max assignment instead of a real recursive insert.

Forgetting that the current min/max is never stored inside a cluster or the summary — Member, Successor and Predecessor must special-case equality with $V.min$/$V.max$ before recursing, and Delete must restore a new min/max from the cluster or summary structure once the cached one is removed.

Using a universe size $u$ that is not of the form $2^{2^k}$ — $high$, $low$ and $index$ only invert cleanly when $\sqrt u$ is itself an integer of the same form at every recursive level; picking, say, $u=2^6$ breaks the split partway down.

Treating the $O(\lg\lg u)$ bound for x-fast/y-fast tries as worst-case: it relies on hash tables at every trie level, so it is expected time (or needs a hashing scheme with deterministic worst-case guarantees) rather than the array-indexed vEB tree's true worst-case bound.

Treating a vEB tree as a drop-in replacement for a balanced BST over machine words: at $u=2^{64}$ the naive structure needs on the order of $u$ words of storage regardless of how few keys are actually stored, which is exactly why nobody builds one directly over 64-bit keys.
applications: Cache-oblivious B-trees / static search trees (Bender, Demaine, Farach-Colton): the recursive $\sqrt n$ memory layout from vEB trees, reused as a static array layout rather than a dynamic pointer structure, gives $O(\log_B n)$ search at every block size $B$ simultaneously.

Integer sorting over a bounded universe: inserting $n$ keys then repeatedly extracting the minimum via Successor sorts in $O(n\lg\lg u)$, useful when $u$ is too large for counting sort's $O(u)$ array but small enough that $\lg\lg u$ beats $\lg n$.

x-fast and y-fast tries are the standard theoretical answer to predecessor/longest-prefix-style queries in $O(\lg\lg u)$ time and $O(n)$ space, and the usual next step in an algorithms course after vEB trees, on the way to fusion trees and predecessor-problem lower bounds.

vEB trees themselves see essentially no production use — their role today is pedagogical: they are the canonical example of trading a $\sqrt u$-shaped divide-and-conquer for an $O(\lg\lg u)$ bound, a pattern that recurs in succinct and cache-oblivious data structure design.

self_check.question: Insert(V, x) looks like it should touch both V.summary and V.cluster[high(x)] at every level of recursion. Why is its worst-case time still O(lg lg u) rather than O(lg u)?
self_check.answer: Because those two possible recursive calls are mutually exclusive — never both real. If V.cluster[high(x)] is already non-empty, Insert recurses only into that cluster (size √u) and leaves the summary untouched, since high(x) is already marked there from an earlier insertion. If the cluster is empty, Insert does recurse into V.summary (size √u) to mark it, but then sets the cluster's min and max directly — an O(1) assignment, not a recursive insert, since a freshly-touched cluster with one element is exactly what that assignment produces. Either way, exactly one size-√u recursive call happens per level, giving T(u) = T(√u) + O(1), which solves to O(lg lg u) by substituting m = lg u (repeated square-rooting of u becomes repeated halving of m). Dropping the exclusivity — always recursing into both — lets an already-marked summary index get 're-inserted', which recurses further instead of hitting the O(1) empty-structure base case, degrading the recurrence to T(u) = 2T(√u) + O(1) = Θ(lg u).

self_check.question: A vEB tree is built directly over the universe of 64-bit unsigned integers, u = 2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616, to hold n = 1,000 keys. (a) What is lg lg u, the worst-case recursion depth for Successor? (b) Why is this structure not actually buildable regardless of n, and roughly how does a y-fast trie improve on it?
self_check.answer: (a) lg u = 64 and lg 64 = 6, so lg lg u = 6: at most six levels of recursion for any operation, versus 64 bit-comparisons for a balanced BST over the same universe. (b) A vEB tree allocates a cluster array and a summary at every level sized by the universe size at that level, regardless of n, so total space is Θ(u) = Θ(2^64) — even at one byte per slot this has no realistic hardware analogue, let alone at 8 bytes per pointer. A y-fast trie instead sizes its space by n: O(n) = O(1,000) words across the balanced BSTs holding the groups, plus O(n/lg u) ≈ 1,000/64 ≈ 16 leaves in the x-fast trie on top, each costing O(lg u) = O(64) words of hash-table entries — on the order of a few thousand words total, versus the unbuildable Θ(2^64), for the same O(lg lg u) = O(6) time bound.

self_check.question: You need to sort n = 10^6 32-bit unsigned integers (u = 2^32) using as little extra memory as possible while beating comparison sorting's Θ(n lg n). Compare (i) counting sort, (ii) a vEB tree used as a priority queue (insert all n keys, then repeatedly extract the minimum), and (iii) the same idea built on a y-fast trie. Which would you pick, and why?
self_check.answer: (i) Counting sort runs in Θ(n+u) = Θ(10^6 + 2^32) time and space; the u term (about 4.3×10^9) dominates completely, so despite being 'linear' it is far worse here than an n lg n sort — it only wins when u = O(n). (ii) A vEB-tree priority queue sorts in O(n lg lg u) = O(n·5) time (lg lg 2^32 = lg 32 = 5), asymptotically better than n lg n (lg 10^6 ≈ 20), but its own space is Θ(u) = Θ(2^32) words — it has simply moved the u-sized cost from counting sort's array into the vEB tree's cluster/summary arrays. (iii) The y-fast-trie version keeps the same O(n lg lg u) time (same factor of 5) but only O(n) = O(10^6) space, so it is the only option that is both asymptotically fast and memory-proportional to the input; the cost is a larger constant per operation (hashing plus a balanced-BST search, versus plain array indexing) and an expected rather than worst-case time bound. For this n and u, (iii) is the right choice: (i) and (ii) are both ruled out by space, and only (iii) gets the time improvement without paying Θ(u) memory.

key_points: vEB trees support Insert/Delete/Member/Successor/Predecessor in O(lg lg u) over universe {0,...,u-1}.
Recursive split: high(x)=⌊x/√u⌋ picks the cluster, low(x)=x mod √u is the position inside it.
Insert makes exactly one real recursive call per level, into summary xor cluster, never both.
The current min/max is cached at each node, never duplicated inside its own cluster or summary.
Naive space is Θ(u), independent of n; y-fast tries cut this to O(n) at the same O(lg lg u) time.
u must be of the form 2^(2^k) so √u splits evenly at every recursive level.
tagline: A van Emde Boas tree answers predecessor queries over universe size u in O(lg lg u), splitting u recursively into √u clusters of size √u.
tldr: The van Emde Boas tree solves the dynamic predecessor problem — Insert, Delete, Member, Successor, Predecessor — over an integer universe $\{0,\dots,u-1\}$ in $O(\lg\lg u)$ time, by recursively splitting the universe into $\sqrt u$ clusters of size $\sqrt u$ plus a summary marking which clusters are non-empty. The bound comes from making exactly one real recursive call per level; its cost is $\Theta(u)$ space regardless of how many keys are actually stored. x-fast and y-fast tries trade the array-based structure for hash tables and balanced BSTs to bring space down to $O(n)$ at the same asymptotic time.
